title: Differentiation Rules
summary: Instead of limits every time, use rules: the power rule $\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}$, constant-multiple and sum rules, the product rule, and the quotient rule. Together they differentiate any polynomial or rational function quickly.

power rule.plain: Differentiate a power by dropping the exponent out front and lowering it by one.

constant multiple rule.plain: A constant factor stays put through differentiation.

sum rule.plain: Differentiate a sum term by term.

product rule.plain: Differentiating a product mixes each factor with the other's derivative.

quotient rule.plain: A rule for the derivative of a fraction of functions.

polynomial.plain: A sum of power terms like $3x^2-5x+1$.
polynomial.in_class: Differentiate term by term with the power rule.

constant rule.plain: The derivative of a constant is zero.

concept_sections.heading: Power, constant, and sum rules
concept_sections.explanation: The workhorses: $\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}$, constants pull out, and sums differentiate term by term. A constant alone has derivative $0$.
math_steps: Bring the exponent down and subtract one: $x^n\to nx^{n-1}$.

concept_sections.heading: Negative and fractional powers
concept_sections.explanation: The power rule works for any real exponent. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: $\sqrt{x}=x^{1/2}$, $1/x^3=x^{-3}$.
math_steps: Rewrite as $x^n$ with $n$ possibly negative or fractional.
Rewrite back with roots/fractions if desired.

concept_sections.heading: The product rule
concept_sections.explanation: The derivative of a product is not the product of derivatives. Use $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$ — differentiate one factor at a time and keep the other.

concept_sections.heading: The quotient rule
concept_sections.explanation: For a ratio, $\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)'=\dfrac{f'g-fg'}{g^2}$ — 'low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared'. Order matters because of the subtraction.

concept_sections.heading: Higher-order derivatives
concept_sections.explanation: Differentiate again to get $f''$, and again for $f'''$. The second derivative measures how the slope itself changes — concavity and acceleration.

real_world_examples.title: Acceleration from position
real_world_examples.scenario: A drone's height is a function of time.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The first derivative is velocity, the second is acceleration — higher-order derivatives with physical meaning.

real_world_examples.title: Revenue = price × quantity
real_world_examples.scenario: A shop's revenue depends on two changing quantities.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The product rule differentiates $R=p\cdot q$ when both price and quantity vary with time.

real_world_examples.title: Fuel efficiency
real_world_examples.scenario: Distance per gallon changes with speed.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Rates that are ratios (miles per gallon) differentiate with the quotient rule when both parts vary.
